title: Valsartan and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Dizziness, HCT and Entresto
excerpt: Can you drink on valsartan? How alcohol and this ARB lower blood pressure together, what changes with Diovan HCT, Exforge, and Entresto, which hangover painkillers to avoid, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on valsartan? How alcohol affects blood pressure on Diovan, Diovan HCT, Exforge, and Entresto, plus hangover painkillers and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most people who take valsartan can have an occasional drink, and there's no toxic chemical reaction between the two. The real issue is that alcohol and valsartan both lower your blood pressure, so together they can drop it further than you expect. That usually shows up as dizziness or light-headedness, especially when you stand up, and occasionally as fainting. Over weeks and months, regular heavy drinking does the opposite and pushes blood pressure back up, working against the very thing valsartan is treating. The combination pills need more care: valsartan with hydrochlorothiazide (Diovan HCT) adds a water pill, valsartan with amlodipine (Exforge) adds a second blood vessel relaxer, and sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) is a heart failure medicine, where alcohol is a bigger concern in its own right.

**The quick rules:** Keep to light or moderate drinking, which US dietary guidelines define as up to one drink a day for women and up to two for men. Have your first drink with food, sip water between drinks, and get up slowly from a chair or bed. Don't skip your valsartan to "make room" for a night out. Don't reach for ibuprofen or naproxen for a hangover headache without checking with your pharmacist first. If you take Entresto for heart failure, ask your cardiologist directly how much alcohol, if any, is right for you, because the answer is often "less than you'd guess."

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history and your full medication list. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on valsartan if** you take it for heart failure (including as Entresto), take a combination pill with a water pill or amlodipine, have kidney disease, have been told your potassium runs high, have diabetes, or have had dizzy spells or fainting since starting the medicine. **Get urgent care (call 911 in the US) if** you faint, have chest pain, a very slow or very irregular heartbeat, sudden shortness of breath, severe weakness, confusion, or swelling of your lips, tongue, face, or throat.

## How Valsartan Works, in Plain Words

Valsartan (brand name Diovan) belongs to a group of blood pressure medicines called **angiotensin II receptor blockers**, usually shortened to **ARBs**. It's in the same family as losartan, irbesartan, olmesartan, candesartan, and telmisartan.

Your body makes a hormone called **angiotensin II**. It tightens blood vessels and tells your kidneys to hold on to salt and water, and both of those raise blood pressure. Valsartan blocks the receptors that angiotensin II normally plugs into. Your blood vessels relax, your kidneys let go of a little more salt and water, and your blood pressure comes down.

Doctors prescribe valsartan for three main reasons:

- **High blood pressure (hypertension)**, the most common use.
- **Heart failure**, where it reduces strain on a weakened heart. In heart failure it's now very often given in combination with sacubitril as Entresto.
- **After a heart attack**, in some people whose heart pumping has been weakened.

That third and second group matter for this article. If you take valsartan for your heart rather than just for blood pressure, the conversation about alcohol is different, and we cover it in its own section below.

One useful detail: valsartan is mostly cleared from the body unchanged, through bile and urine, rather than being heavily broken down by liver enzymes. That's part of why alcohol doesn't meaningfully change how much valsartan ends up in your blood. The interaction is about what the two do to your blood pressure and fluid balance, not about one drug blocking the other's breakdown.

## Why Valsartan and Alcohol Can Be a Problem: The Real Mechanism

There are three separate things going on, and they happen on different timescales.

### 1. In the first few hours: two blood-pressure-lowering effects at once

Alcohol widens (dilates) blood vessels in the short term. That's why some people get a warm, flushed face after a drink. Wider vessels mean lower pressure for a few hours. Valsartan is already holding your blood vessels in a more relaxed state. Stack the two, and your blood pressure can dip lower than your body is used to.

Most of the time you won't notice. When you do, it's usually in a specific moment: standing up quickly after sitting for a while, getting out of a hot tub or shower, or walking to the bathroom in the middle of the night. When you stand, gravity pulls blood toward your legs, and your body normally tightens blood vessels within seconds to keep blood flowing to your brain. Valsartan and alcohol both blunt that response. The result is a few seconds of dizziness, tunnel vision, or a "head rush." Doctors call this **orthostatic hypotension**, which simply means a drop in blood pressure on standing.

For most people this is a nuisance. The real danger is falling, especially for older adults, people who are already a bit unsteady, or anyone who's had several drinks.

### 2. The next day: dehydration and your kidneys

Alcohol makes you pee more. It does this by suppressing a hormone called vasopressin (also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Add a warm room, dancing, or a bout of vomiting, and you can wake up properly dehydrated.

Dehydration lowers blood pressure on its own. It also matters for the kidneys. ARBs like valsartan change how blood flows through the tiny filters in your kidneys. That's usually fine and even protective, but when you're very low on fluid, the kidneys rely more on angiotensin II to keep filtering. With that hormone blocked, a dehydrated person on an ARB is more likely to see a temporary dip in kidney function. The Diovan prescribing information warns about low blood pressure in people who are "volume-depleted," meaning low on fluid or salt, and that's exactly what a rough hangover can do to you.

This is also why many doctors and pharmacists use "sick day rules": if you're vomiting or have diarrhea and can't keep fluids down, call them about pausing certain medicines (ARBs, ACE inhibitors, water pills, and some diabetes drugs) until you're eating and drinking normally again. That advice applies just as much to a bad hangover as to a stomach bug.

### 3. Over weeks and months: alcohol pushes blood pressure up

This is the part that surprises people. While one or two drinks can lower blood pressure for a few hours, **regular heavy drinking raises it**. Large studies and reviews have consistently found that blood pressure climbs as average alcohol intake climbs, and that cutting back in heavy drinkers brings it down. The American Heart Association and other major bodies list limiting alcohol as one of the core lifestyle steps for managing high blood pressure.

So there's a tug-of-war. Valsartan is lowering your blood pressure every day, and a heavy drinking pattern is pushing it back up. People sometimes conclude their medicine "isn't working" and end up on higher doses or extra drugs, when cutting back would have done much of the job. Our guide to [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) goes into this in more detail.

## What the Official Label Says

The US prescribing information for Diovan doesn't list alcohol as a specific drug interaction, and there's no warning saying you must avoid it completely. What the label does warn about is **symptomatic low blood pressure**, particularly in people who are low on fluid or salt, and it lists dizziness as a common side effect. It also warns about **high potassium** and **changes in kidney function**, and about combining valsartan with NSAID pain relievers.

The combination products carry their own warnings. Labels for hydrochlorothiazide-containing products note that alcohol can make dizziness on standing worse. That's why Diovan HCT and Exforge HCT need a bit more care than valsartan on its own.

In plain terms: the label's concern is your blood pressure dropping too far and your kidneys getting strained when you're dried out. Alcohol happens to push in both of those directions.

## Can You Drink on Valsartan? A Practical Answer

For most people taking valsartan for high blood pressure, with normal kidney function and no history of fainting, **light to moderate drinking is generally considered acceptable**. Many doctors will say something like "a drink or two is fine, just be sensible." That's a reasonable starting point, but it isn't a blanket rule, and your doctor is the one who should set your personal limit.

A few things change the answer:

- **How much you drink in one sitting.** One glass of wine with dinner is a very different situation from five drinks at a party. The blood pressure dip, the dehydration, and the fall risk all scale with the amount.
- **What else you take.** A water pill, amlodipine, a beta-blocker, alpha-blockers for prostate symptoms, or erectile dysfunction drugs all add their own blood-pressure-lowering effect.
- **Why you take it.** Valsartan for heart failure is a different conversation, covered below.
- **How new it is.** The first couple of weeks on valsartan, or after a dose increase, are when dizziness is most likely. It's sensible to hold off on drinking, or keep it very light, until you know how the medicine affects you.

## How Long After Taking Valsartan Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period, and spacing your drinks away from your dose doesn't make much difference. Valsartan reaches its peak level in the blood a few hours after you take it, but its blood-pressure-lowering effect lasts around the clock, which is the whole point of a once- or twice-daily medicine. By the time you're having a drink in the evening, valsartan is still working whether you took it that morning or the night before.

What you can control:

- **Keep taking your dose at your usual time.** Consistency matters more than timing around drinks.
- **If you take valsartan at night,** be extra careful about getting up quickly after drinking, because you'll be stacking evening alcohol with the medicine, and the nighttime bathroom trip is a classic moment for a dizzy fall.
- **Don't move your dose to the morning after a night out "to be safe"** without asking your pharmacist. Shuffling doses around can leave gaps or doubles.

## Should You Skip a Dose Before Drinking?

No. This is one of the most common questions, and the answer is clear. Skipping valsartan lets your blood pressure drift up, and for people taking it for heart failure, missed doses can mean fluid building up again. It also doesn't make drinking meaningfully safer, because the effect carries over from earlier doses.

The one time to consider pausing is the "sick day" situation: if you're vomiting or have diarrhea and can't keep fluids down, after drinking or for any other reason, call your doctor or pharmacist. They may tell you to hold your dose until you're eating and drinking normally. Make that call rather than deciding on your own.

## Diovan HCT (Valsartan-Hydrochlorothiazide) and Alcohol

Diovan HCT and its generics combine valsartan with **hydrochlorothiazide**, a water pill (diuretic). The water pill helps lower blood pressure by making your kidneys flush out more salt and water.

That makes alcohol a bigger deal, for two reasons:

1. **Double the fluid loss.** Alcohol already makes you pee more. A water pill does the same. Together, it's easier to end up dehydrated, and dehydration on an ARB is the kidney-strain situation described above.
2. **More dizziness on standing.** Thiazide labels specifically mention that alcohol can make orthostatic hypotension worse.

Hydrochlorothiazide can also lower sodium and potassium levels, and heavy drinking, vomiting, and diarrhea can push those levels around further. Valsartan tends to nudge potassium up while the water pill nudges it down, so the net effect varies from person to person. That's one reason your doctor checks blood tests.

If you take Diovan HCT and drink, keep it light, alternate every drink with a full glass of water, and be extra careful standing up.

## Exforge (Amlodipine-Valsartan) and Alcohol

Exforge and its generics combine valsartan with **amlodipine**, a calcium channel blocker. Amlodipine lowers blood pressure in a different way: it relaxes the muscle in artery walls directly. Exforge HCT adds hydrochlorothiazide on top of both.

With alcohol, the effects add up. You now have three things relaxing your blood vessels: valsartan, amlodipine, and the alcohol itself. In practice, people on Exforge often notice:

- **More dizziness and light-headedness**, especially on standing.
- **More flushing and warmth**, since amlodipine and alcohol both widen blood vessels in the skin.
- **Worse ankle and foot swelling.** Ankle swelling is one of amlodipine's best-known side effects, and an evening of drinking, salty bar food, and standing around can make it more noticeable the next morning.

None of this means you can't drink on Exforge, but you have less margin than someone on valsartan alone. Our article on [amlodipine and alcohol](/never-hungover/amlodipine-and-alcohol) covers that half of the combination in more depth.

## Entresto (Sacubitril-Valsartan) and Alcohol

Entresto is valsartan combined with **sacubitril**, a drug that blocks an enzyme called neprilysin. Neprilysin normally breaks down natural hormones that help the body get rid of excess salt and water and relax blood vessels. Blocking it lets those helpful hormones stick around longer. Entresto is used mainly for **heart failure**, and it lowers blood pressure more than valsartan alone.

Here the question isn't really about a drug interaction. It's about alcohol and heart failure:

- **Alcohol can weaken heart muscle.** Long-term heavy drinking is a recognized cause of a type of heart failure called alcoholic cardiomyopathy. Even in people whose heart failure has another cause, heavy drinking can make it worse.
- **Alcohol can trigger irregular heart rhythms.** Binge drinking is linked to atrial fibrillation (sometimes called "holiday heart"), and people with heart failure handle a rhythm problem less well.
- **Fluid matters a lot in heart failure.** Many people with heart failure are told to limit total fluids and salt. A night of beer and salty snacks can mean extra fluid on board, ankle swelling, and shortness of breath.
- **Low blood pressure is already the most common issue with Entresto.** The label lists hypotension as a key warning. Adding alcohol on top makes dizziness and falls more likely.

Major heart failure guidance generally advises people with heart failure to limit alcohol, and to avoid it entirely if alcohol has played a role in their heart failure. The right amount for you depends on your type of heart failure, how stable you are, and your other medicines. **If you take Entresto, ask your cardiologist or heart failure nurse directly.** Don't assume the "two drinks is fine" advice for blood pressure applies to you.

Entresto also carries a warning about **angioedema**, a serious swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat. Alcohol doesn't cause it, but if you ever notice that kind of swelling, get emergency help right away and don't brush it off as an allergic reaction to something you ate or drank.

## Valsartan and Alcohol Side Effects: What You Might Notice

Most people who have a drink or two on valsartan feel nothing unusual. When the combination does cause problems, these are the usual signs:

- **Dizziness or light-headedness**, especially when standing up.
- **Feeling faint**, or briefly blacking out after getting up.
- **Tiredness or unusual weakness.**
- **A faster heartbeat**, as your body tries to make up for the lower pressure.
- **Worse next-day dehydration**: headache, dry mouth, dark urine, peeing less than usual.
- **Blurry vision for a moment** on standing.

If you notice these, sit or lie down right away, drink some water, and stand up slowly in stages when you feel better. If it keeps happening, tell your doctor. You may need a dose adjustment, and it's useful for them to know.

## When to Get Help Right Away

> **Call 911 (US) or go to the emergency department if you:**
> - Faint or pass out, especially if you hit your head.
> - Have chest pain or pressure.
> - Have a very slow, very fast, or very irregular heartbeat.
> - Have sudden shortness of breath, or can't lie flat because of breathlessness (a warning sign in heart failure).
> - Notice swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat, or trouble swallowing or breathing.
> - Have severe muscle weakness or a heartbeat that feels "off," which can be signs of very high potassium.
> - Are confused, very drowsy, or can't keep any fluids down for many hours.
>
> **Call your doctor or pharmacist the same day if you:** keep getting dizzy spells, pee much less than usual, notice new or worsening ankle swelling, or gain more than a few pounds over a day or two (if you have heart failure, follow the weight rule your care team gave you).

These signs aren't about how much you drank. They're about how your body is coping, and they deserve attention whether you had one drink or several.

## Hangover Painkillers on Valsartan: What to Take and What to Avoid

This is where a lot of people run into trouble without realizing it.

**NSAIDs** (ibuprofen, naproxen, high-dose aspirin) are the most common hangover painkillers, and they're the ones to be careful with. The Diovan label warns that NSAIDs can make valsartan less effective and, especially in people who are older, dehydrated, or have kidney problems, can worsen kidney function. The combination of an ARB, a water pill, and an NSAID is one that pharmacists sometimes call the "triple whammy" because of its kidney risk. A dehydrated hangover morning is exactly the wrong time to take that gamble. Our guide on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) explains the stomach side of the problem too.

**Acetaminophen (Tylenol)** is usually the preferred pain reliever for people on blood pressure medicines, because it doesn't affect blood pressure or the kidneys the way NSAIDs do. It has its own alcohol caution for the liver, so stick to a single standard dose, eat first, and wait until the alcohol has cleared. If you drink heavily on a regular basis, ask your doctor before using it. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) covers the details.

**Decongestants** like pseudoephedrine and phenylephrine, found in many "cold and flu" and "sinus" products, can raise blood pressure. If you're grabbing a combination product for a stuffy, achy morning, read the label.

When in doubt, ask the pharmacist at the counter. It takes two minutes, and they can see your full list.

## Potassium, Coconut Water, and Salt Substitutes

Valsartan can raise potassium levels, because blocking angiotensin II reduces a hormone (aldosterone) that normally helps the kidneys get rid of potassium. For most people the rise is small. It's larger in people with kidney disease, diabetes, or heart failure, and in those who also take potassium-sparing water pills like spironolactone.

That's relevant to hangover habits. A lot of popular hangover fixes are loaded with potassium:

- **Coconut water** is naturally high in potassium.
- **Some electrolyte drinks and powders** contain significant potassium.
- **Salt substitutes** (such as "lite salt" or potassium chloride products) replace sodium with potassium.
- **Potassium supplements** taken "to replace what alcohol flushed out."

An occasional glass of coconut water is unlikely to be a problem for someone with healthy kidneys. But if you're on valsartan or Entresto and have kidney disease, or have been told your potassium runs high, check with your doctor before making these a regular part of your recovery routine. Plain water with some food, or a standard electrolyte drink your doctor is happy with, is a safer default. See our article on [potassium and alcohol](/never-hungover/potassium-and-alcohol) for more.

## Does Alcohol Make Valsartan Less Effective?

Not directly. Alcohol doesn't block valsartan or change how it's absorbed or cleared in any way that matters at moderate intake.

The indirect effect is the one to watch. Regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure by itself, which can make it look like valsartan has stopped working. Heavy drinking also makes it easier to forget or skip doses, and it often comes with salty food, which raises blood pressure too. If your home readings have crept up, an honest look at how much you're drinking is worth doing before assuming you need a stronger medicine.

## The 2018 Valsartan Recall: Is It Still a Concern?

If you've searched for valsartan, you've probably seen mention of the recall. In 2018, the FDA announced recalls of certain generic valsartan products after a probable cancer-causing impurity (NDMA, part of a group called nitrosamines) was found in some batches from particular manufacturers. Recalls later extended to some losartan and irbesartan products.

This has nothing to do with alcohol, but it's a common worry. The FDA has since tightened testing requirements for nitrosamine impurities, and recalled batches were removed from the market. If you're unsure about your current supply, your pharmacist can tell you the manufacturer and check it against the FDA's records. Don't stop taking valsartan on your own because of the recall, since uncontrolled blood pressure carries its own real risks.

## How Valsartan Compares With Losartan and Other Blood Pressure Medicines

All ARBs behave similarly with alcohol: the same additive blood pressure drop, the same dehydration and kidney concerns, and the same issue with NSAIDs and potassium. If you've read our [losartan and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/losartan-and-alcohol), almost everything there applies to valsartan too.

ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril work on the same hormone system one step earlier, and they carry similar alcohol considerations. Our [lisinopril and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/lisinopril-and-alcohol) covers that family. Beta-blockers like metoprolol are a different story, since they also slow your heart rate, which can change how your body handles a blood pressure dip.

The bigger differences come from what valsartan is combined with (a water pill, amlodipine, or sacubitril) and why you take it, not from the ARB itself.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

Take extra care, and talk to your doctor before drinking, if you:

- Take valsartan for **heart failure** or after a **heart attack**, or take **Entresto**.
- Take a **combination pill** (Diovan HCT, Exforge, Exforge HCT).
- Have **chronic kidney disease** or have been told your kidney numbers are off.
- Have been told your **potassium is high**, or take spironolactone, eplerenone, or potassium supplements.
- Are **over 65**, or have had falls or dizzy spells.
- Have **diabetes**, especially if you take insulin or a sulfonylurea, since alcohol can also cause low blood sugar.
- Take other medicines that lower blood pressure, such as **alpha-blockers** for prostate symptoms (tamsulosin, doxazosin), **nitrates** for chest pain, or **erectile dysfunction drugs**.
- Are **pregnant or could become pregnant**. Valsartan carries a boxed warning against use in pregnancy because it can harm a developing baby, separate from any alcohol question. If you find out you're pregnant, contact your doctor promptly.

## Practical Tips for a Night Out on Valsartan

If you and your doctor are comfortable with you drinking, these habits help you avoid the most common problems:

1. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows how quickly alcohol hits your bloodstream, which softens the blood pressure dip.
2. **Pace yourself.** Aim for no more than one drink an hour, and decide your limit before you start.
3. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water for every drink helps offset alcohol's fluid loss, which matters more if you take a water pill.
4. **Stand up slowly.** Sit on the edge of the bed or chair for a few seconds before getting up, especially at night.
5. **Skip the hot tub or sauna after drinking.** Heat widens blood vessels too, and stacking heat, alcohol, and valsartan is a reliable way to feel faint.
6. **Watch the salty snacks,** especially if you have heart failure or take Exforge and get ankle swelling.
7. **Take your medicine as normal** the next day, unless you're vomiting or can't keep fluids down, in which case call your doctor or pharmacist.
8. **Choose acetaminophen over ibuprofen** for a hangover headache, in a single sensible dose, after you've eaten.
9. **Keep an eye on home blood pressure readings.** If your numbers rise over weeks when you've been drinking more, that's useful information for your next appointment.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's often sold as a hangover supplement. Research on it, mostly from animal and lab studies with limited human data, has looked at its effects on alcohol metabolism and liver health. It's an interesting area, but it's important to be clear about what it can and can't do for someone on valsartan.

**There is no good evidence that DHM changes the interaction between alcohol and valsartan.** It won't stop the blood pressure dip, it won't prevent dizziness on standing, it won't protect your kidneys from dehydration, and it doesn't make it safe to drink more than your doctor has advised. There's also very little research on DHM taken alongside blood pressure or heart failure medicines, so if you want to try it, run it past your pharmacist first, the same way you would with any supplement.

If you've checked and you want to try it for the general hangover side of things, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about DHM alongside common medicines, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits that matter most: drinking less, drinking slower, eating, and staying hydrated.

## The Bottom Line

- Valsartan and alcohol don't have a toxic chemical reaction, but **both lower blood pressure**, so together they can cause dizziness, light-headedness on standing, and occasionally fainting.
- **Light to moderate drinking is generally acceptable** for people taking valsartan for high blood pressure, but your doctor should set your personal limit.
- **Combination pills need more care**: Diovan HCT adds dehydration risk, Exforge adds more blood vessel relaxation and ankle swelling, and Entresto means you're managing heart failure, where alcohol is a bigger concern.
- **Don't skip doses** to make room for drinking. Do call your doctor if you're vomiting or can't keep fluids down.
- **Avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen** for hangovers without checking first, and be careful with potassium-heavy hangover drinks if your kidneys or potassium are an issue.
- **Regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure** and works against your medicine. Cutting back is one of the most effective things you can do for your numbers.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking valsartan?**

Most people taking valsartan for high blood pressure can have an occasional drink, usually within moderate limits (up to one drink a day for women and two for men). There's no toxic reaction, but alcohol and valsartan both lower blood pressure, so the combination can cause dizziness or light-headedness, especially when standing. Ask your doctor what limit is right for you, particularly if you have heart failure, kidney disease, or take a combination pill.

**What are the side effects of mixing valsartan and alcohol?**

The most common effects are dizziness and light-headedness on standing, feeling faint, tiredness, a faster heartbeat, and worse next-day dehydration. Fainting, chest pain, a very irregular heartbeat, sudden shortness of breath, or swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat need emergency care right away.

**How long after taking valsartan can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period, and spacing drinks away from your dose doesn't change much, because valsartan's blood-pressure-lowering effect lasts around the clock. Keep taking your dose at your usual time, drink moderately, eat with your drinks, and stand up slowly. If you take it at night, be especially careful getting up to use the bathroom after drinking.

**Can I drink alcohol on valsartan HCT (Diovan HCT)?**

It needs more care than valsartan alone. The hydrochlorothiazide in Diovan HCT is a water pill, so alcohol and the medicine both make you lose fluid, which makes dehydration and dizziness on standing more likely. Thiazide labels note that alcohol can worsen that standing dizziness. If you drink, keep it light, alternate each drink with water, and ask your doctor what's reasonable for you.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol with amlodipine and valsartan (Exforge)?**

You have less margin than with valsartan alone. Valsartan, amlodipine, and alcohol all relax blood vessels, so dizziness, flushing, and ankle swelling are more likely after drinking. Light drinking may be acceptable for some people, but check with your doctor, and be extra careful standing up and with salty food.

**Can you drink alcohol on Entresto (sacubitril/valsartan)?**

Ask your cardiologist directly. Entresto is mainly a heart failure medicine, and heart failure guidance generally advises limiting alcohol, or avoiding it entirely if alcohol contributed to your heart failure. Alcohol can weaken heart muscle, trigger irregular rhythms, add fluid, and worsen the low blood pressure that is already Entresto's most common side effect.

**Should I skip my valsartan dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Skipping a dose lets your blood pressure rise and, in heart failure, can let fluid build up, and it doesn't make drinking meaningfully safer. Take it as usual. The exception is if you're vomiting or have diarrhea and can't keep fluids down; then call your doctor or pharmacist about pausing it until you're eating and drinking normally.

**Can I take ibuprofen for a hangover while on valsartan?**

Check with your pharmacist first. The valsartan label warns that NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen can reduce its effect and can worsen kidney function, especially when you're dehydrated, older, or also taking a water pill. A single sensible dose of acetaminophen (Tylenol), taken after eating and once the alcohol has cleared, is usually the preferred option for people on blood pressure medicines.

**Does alcohol make valsartan less effective?**

Not directly. Alcohol doesn't meaningfully change how valsartan is absorbed or cleared. But regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure on its own, which can make it look like the medicine isn't working. Cutting back on heavy drinking is one of the most effective ways to improve blood pressure control.

**Does DHM help if I drink while taking valsartan?**

There is no good evidence that DHM changes the interaction between alcohol and valsartan. It won't prevent the blood pressure dip, dizziness, or dehydration, and it doesn't make it safe to drink more. There's also little research on DHM alongside blood pressure medicines, so check with your pharmacist before adding it.

Thiazide labels note that alcohol can worsen that standing dizziness. If you drink, keep it light, alternate each drink with water, and ask your doctor what's reasonable for you.

faq.question: Is it safe to drink alcohol with amlodipine and valsartan (Exforge)?
faq.answer: You have less margin than with valsartan alone. Valsartan, amlodipine, and alcohol all relax blood vessels, so dizziness, flushing, and ankle swelling are more likely after drinking. Light drinking may be acceptable for some people, but check with your doctor, and be extra careful standing up and with salty food.

faq.question: Can you drink alcohol on Entresto (sacubitril/valsartan)?
faq.answer: Ask your cardiologist directly. Entresto is mainly a heart failure medicine, and heart failure guidance generally advises limiting alcohol, or avoiding it entirely if alcohol contributed to your heart failure. Alcohol can weaken heart muscle, trigger irregular rhythms, add fluid, and worsen the low blood pressure that is already Entresto's most common side effect.

faq.question: Should I skip my valsartan dose if I'm going to drink?
faq.answer: No. Skipping a dose lets your blood pressure rise and, in heart failure, can let fluid build up, and it doesn't make drinking meaningfully safer. Take it as usual. The exception is if you're vomiting or have diarrhea and can't keep fluids down; then call your doctor or pharmacist about pausing it until you're eating and drinking normally.

faq.question: Can I take ibuprofen for a hangover while on valsartan?
faq.answer: Check with your pharmacist first. The valsartan label warns that NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen can reduce its effect and can worsen kidney function, especially when you're dehydrated, older, or also taking a water pill. A single sensible dose of acetaminophen (Tylenol), taken after eating and once the alcohol has cleared, is usually the preferred option for people on blood pressure medicines.

faq.question: Does alcohol make valsartan less effective?
faq.answer: Not directly. Alcohol doesn't meaningfully change how valsartan is absorbed or cleared. But regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure on its own, which can make it look like the medicine isn't working. Cutting back on heavy drinking is one of the most effective ways to improve blood pressure control.

faq.question: Does DHM help if I drink while taking valsartan?
faq.answer: There is no good evidence that DHM changes the interaction between alcohol and valsartan. It won't prevent the blood pressure dip, dizziness, or dehydration, and it doesn't make it safe to drink more. There's also little research on DHM alongside blood pressure medicines, so check with your pharmacist before adding it.
